sentence: Recent systems such as LogRules (Huang et al., 2025) achieve strong performance by separating log parsing into two stages: an induction stage where an LLM generates parsing rules from labeled examples, and a deduction stage where a smaller model applies these rules to new logs.
title: Logrules: Enhancing log analysis capability of large language models through rules

sentence: Because the induction LLM processes user-provided examples that are concatenated into natural-language prompts, an attacker who can influence even a small number of these examples may manipulate the generated rules through indirect prompt injection (Greshake et al., 2023).
title: Not What You’ve Signed Up For: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection

sentence: We design three payload formats that exploit indirect prompt injection to manipulate rule generation, and evaluate their effectiveness across four poisoning budgets on three benchmark datasets from Loghub (Zhu et al., 2020).
title: Loghub: A large collection of system log datasets for ai-driven log analytics

sentence: Log parsing transforms semi-structured log messages into structured representations, serving as a prerequisite for downstream log analysis tasks such as anomaly detection and root cause analysis (Zhu et al., 2020).
title: Loghub: A large collection of system log datasets for ai-driven log analytics

sentence: Traditional approaches rely on human-crafted rules or learning-based models with limited training data, which struggle with the diversity and complexity of modern log data (Jiang et al., 2023b).
title: A Large-Scale Evaluation for Log Parsing Techniques: How Far Are We?

sentence: The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has introduced new paradigms for log parsing that leverage pre-trained knowledge about code and logging patterns (Beck et al., 2025).
title: System log parsing with large language models: A review

sentence: Prompt-based methods such as Le & Zhang (2023) and Xu et al. (2023) leverage few-shot learning to extract log templates without extensive training data.
title: Log parsing with prompt-based few-shot learning

sentence: Prompt-based methods such as Le & Zhang (2023) and Xu et al. (2023) leverage few-shot learning to extract log templates without extensive training data.
title: Prompting for automatic log template extraction

sentence: LILAC (Jiang et al., 2023a) introduces an adaptive parsing cache that stores and refines LLM-generated templates, achieving significant improvements in parsing accuracy while reducing LLM query overhead.
title: Lilac: Log parsing using llms with adaptive parsing cache

sentence: Wu et al. (2024) propose self-generated in-context learning with self-correction mechanisms to improve parsing robustness.
title: Log parsing using llms with self-generated in-context learning and self-correction

sentence: LogRules (Huang et al., 2025) represents a distinct paradigm that separates log parsing into induction and deduction stages.
title: Logrules: Enhancing log analysis capability of large language models through rules

sentence: Greshake et al. (2023) introduce indirect prompt injection, where attackers embed malicious payloads in external data sources (e.g., web pages, documents) that LLM-integrated applications retrieve and process.
title: Not What You’ve Signed Up For: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection

sentence: Wallace et al. (2024) propose the instruction hierarchy framework to defend against such attacks by training LLMs to prioritize privileged (system) instructions over user or external inputs.
title: The instruction hierarchy: Training llms to prioritize privileged instructions

sentence: Yi et al. (2024) provide a comprehensive survey of jailbreak attacks that bypass LLM safety guardrails through various techniques including role-playing, encoding, and multi-turn conversations.
title: Jailbreak attacks and defenses against large language models: A survey

sentence: Wallace et al. (2021) demonstrate concealed poisoning attacks on NLP models where adversaries inject trigger phrases that cause targeted misbehavior while maintaining normal performance on clean inputs.
title: Concealed data poisoning attacks on nlp models. pp. 139–150

sentence: Zhou et al. (2024) extend this to LLM instruction tuning, showing that poisoned fine-tuning data can manipulate downstream model behavior.
title: Learning to poison large language models for downstream manipulation

sentence: Guo et al. (2021) provide an overview of backdoor attacks against deep neural networks, categorizing attack strategies and defense mechanisms.
title: An overview of backdoor attacks against deep neural networks and possible defences
